sections.heading: The oath by Styx
sections.translation:
There lives a goddess hated by the immortals:
dread Styx, eldest daughter of Oceanus,
the river that flows back on itself.
Far from the other gods she lives in a splendid house,
with towering rocks above it and silver pillars
supporting it on every side, reaching toward the sky.

Rarely does swift-footed Iris, daughter of Thaumas,
come across the sea’s broad back with a message.
But whenever quarrels and strife break out among the immortals,
and one of the gods who live on Olympus tells a lie,
Zeus sends Iris far away to bring back, in a golden jug,
the famous cold water by which the gods swear their great oath.
It trickles down from a high, sheer rock.

Far beneath the earth with its broad roads,
a branch of the sacred river Oceanus
flows through black night.
One tenth of his water has been set apart:
nine parts wind around the earth and the sea’s broad back
in silver swirls, then pour into the sea.
The one remaining part flows from the rock—
a great source of suffering for the gods.

If any immortal who lives on snowy Olympus
pours out this water and swears a false oath over it,
that god lies breathless for a full year.
They never come near ambrosia or nectar to eat or drink,
but lie without breath or speech on a bed spread for them,
wrapped in a dreadful coma.

When that sickness has lasted a full year,
another, harsher ordeal follows.
For nine years the god is cut off from the gods who live forever,
never joining their councils or their feasts
for all those nine years.
In the tenth, they join once more
the gatherings of the immortals who live on Olympus.

Such is the oath the gods established:
the ancient, unfailing water of Styx,
which flows through a harsh and rocky place.
sections.summary: The gods swear their strongest oath by the water of Styx. A god who breaks it lies helpless for a year, then spends nine years apart from the other gods.

cards.label: Styx
cards.general: A goddess and an underworld river. Her water makes the gods’ most binding oath.
cards.here: She lives apart from the other gods, who face severe punishment if they swear falsely by her water.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
cards.here: He is Styx’s father, and her stream receives one tenth of his water.

cards.label: Iris
cards.general: A swift messenger of the gods, associated with the rainbow.
cards.here: Zeus sends her to fetch the water of Styx in a golden jug.

cards.label: Thaumas
cards.general: A sea god and the father of Iris.
cards.here: Hesiod identifies Iris by naming her father.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods, whose weapon is the thunderbolt.
cards.here: He sends for the water when a dispute involves a god’s lie.

cards.label: Olympus
cards.general: The mountain where Zeus and the other ruling gods have their homes.
cards.here: A punished god is excluded from their councils and feasts.

cards.label: Ambrosia and nectar
cards.general: The gods’ food and drink.
cards.here: A god who swears falsely cannot eat or drink them during the year of helplessness.

cards.label: Coma
cards.general: A deep state of unconsciousness in which someone cannot wake or respond.
cards.here: The offending god lies unable to breathe or speak for a full year.

sections.heading: At the world’s limits
sections.translation:
There, side by side, are the sources and the limits
of dark earth, misty Tartarus,
the barren sea and the starry sky:
grim, moldy places that even the gods hate.

There stand marble gates and a bronze threshold,
unshakable, fixed on roots that stretch unbroken below,
grown there of itself.
Beyond the gates, apart from all the other gods,
the Titans live on the far side of gloomy Chaos.

But Cottus and Gyes, the famous allies
of loudly thundering Zeus,
live in homes at the foundations of Oceanus.
As for noble Briareus, the Earth-shaker Poseidon,
whose crashes thunder deep,
made him his son-in-law:
he gave him his daughter Cymopolea to marry.
sections.summary: At the world’s dark limits stand great gates. The Titans live beyond them, while Zeus’s allies have homes near Oceanus. Briareus marries Poseidon’s daughter.

cards.label: Tartarus
cards.general: A vast, dark region far beneath the earth.
cards.here: Its sources and limits lie beside those of earth, sea and sky.

cards.label: Chaos
cards.general: The primordial gap or chasm; the name does not simply mean disorder.
cards.here: The Titans live on the far side of this gloomy gulf.

cards.label: Titans
cards.general: An older generation of gods defeated by Zeus and his allies.
cards.here: They live confined beyond the gates, apart from the other gods.

cards.label: Threshold
cards.general: The sill across the bottom of a doorway.
cards.here: This bronze threshold is firmly rooted in the depths.

cards.label: Cottus and Gyes
cards.general: Two of three giant brothers, each with a hundred hands and fifty heads.
cards.here: They helped Zeus defeat the Titans and now live at Oceanus’s foundations.

cards.label: Briareus
cards.general: The third of the hundred-handed brothers who helped Zeus.
cards.here: Poseidon makes him his son-in-law by giving him Cymopolea in marriage.

cards.label: Poseidon, the Earth-shaker
cards.general: The god of the sea and earthquakes. “Earth-shaker” is one of his titles.
cards.here: The Greek names him by his title; he is Cymopolea’s father.

cards.label: Cymopolea
cards.general: A divine daughter of Poseidon.
cards.here: She becomes Briareus’s wife.

cards.label: Oceanus
cards.general: The divine river that circles the world.
cards.here: Cottus and Gyes have their homes at his foundations.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods, associated with thunder and lightning.
cards.here: Cottus, Gyes and Briareus were his allies against the Titans.

sections.heading: Earth gives birth to Typhoeus
sections.translation:
After Zeus had driven the Titans out of heaven,
vast Gaia gave birth to her youngest child, Typhoeus,
joining in love with Tartarus through golden Aphrodite.

This powerful god had hands strong enough for mighty deeds,
and feet that never tired.
From his shoulders grew a hundred snake heads,
the heads of a terrifying serpent,
flicking their dark tongues.
Fire flashed beneath the brows
of the eyes in those monstrous heads;
from every head fire blazed as he stared.

Voices sounded in all his fearsome heads,
sending out every kind of incredible cry.
Sometimes they spoke so that the gods could understand;
sometimes they sounded like a proud, bellowing bull
whose force could not be held back;
sometimes like a lion with a ruthless heart;
sometimes like puppies—a wonder to hear.
At other times he hissed,
and the tall mountains echoed.

That day something beyond all help would have happened:
Typhoeus would have ruled over mortals and immortals,
if Zeus, the father of gods and humans,
had not been quick to notice.
sections.summary: Gaia and Tartarus have a terrifying child, Typhoeus. With a hundred fiery snake heads and many strange voices, he nearly becomes ruler of gods and humans.

cards.label: Gaia
cards.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
cards.here: She gives birth to Typhoeus, her youngest child.

cards.label: Tartarus
cards.general: Both the deep region beneath the earth and a divine being.
cards.here: He is Typhoeus’s father.

cards.label: Typhoeus
cards.general: A monstrous divine being who challenges Zeus for rule.
cards.here: He has a hundred snake heads, blazing eyes and voices that imitate many creatures.

cards.label: Aphrodite
cards.general: The goddess of love and sexual desire, often called “golden.”
cards.here: Her power brings Gaia and Tartarus together.

cards.label: Zeus
cards.general: The ruler of the gods, called the father of gods and humans.
cards.here: He notices the threat before Typhoeus can take control.

cards.label: Titans
cards.general: The older gods whom Zeus defeated in a war for power.
cards.here: Their defeat comes before Typhoeus’s birth.

cards.label: Mortals and immortals
cards.general: Humans, who die, and gods, who live forever.
cards.here: Typhoeus nearly gains power over both.

uncertainties: Line 774 is marked for deletion in the preceding context. It is omitted and falls outside the assigned sections.
In line 811, the word translated “marble” can also suggest shining or gleaming gates.
The wording about Typhoeus’s hands in line 823 is difficult. “Hands strong enough for mighty deeds” gives its likely sense.
